In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
metacognition is a human capacity, but one that develops over time, with some individuals showing greater capacities than others.

there is evidence for metacognitive processes in children and adults, but that the evidence is not yet sufficient to conclude that there are qualitative differences in metacognitive development between childhood and adulthood.
metacognitive abilities develop gradually and that the development is not complete until the end of adolescence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
metacognition emerges in early childhood, is refined in middle childhood, undergoes a major transformation during adolescence, and continues to develop throughout adulthood.
metacognition is a process that develops throughout life and that it is a process that can be enhanced by experience and training.

metacognition is a process that can be observed at many different levels of complexity. It may be as simple as a child who is learning to read saying, "I know this word, but I don't know how to spell it" and then using a strategy to figure it out.
The main takeaway from our work is that
metacognition is not a single process but rather an umbrella term that encompasses many different kinds of processes.

metacognition is an important and pervasive phenomenon in children's learning and that children's metacognitive skills are not simply a function of age but are influenced by a variety of other factors, including the type of knowledge to be acquired, the nature of the learning task, and the type of metacognitive support provided.
metacognitive processes are not simply a matter of "thinking about thinking," but rather involve the executive control of firstorder thought processes. See id. at 282 2009
